text: Akbar challenges Birbal to find the true merchant.
Birbal defines a true merchant as one who sells what cannot be bought with gold or silver.
Merchants from across the kingdom arrive at court, each claiming to have the item Birbal described.
Birbal rejects all merchants as not true merchants.
An old man claims to offer something more valuable than gold or jewels.
Birbal acknowledges the old man's wisdom about time being the most precious gift.
The crowd is left in silence after Birbal's final judgment on the merchants.
An old man arrives at court claiming to sell time.
Birbal acknowledges the wisdom of the old man's claim about time.
The merchants are left speechless by Birbal’s insight into the value of time.
Birbal promises to continue searching for the true merchant, now understanding that it may not be a physical item.
The old man's identity and background remain unknown to all in court.
Time is presented as the only treasure that cannot be stolen or stored.
Akbar asks Birbal about true friendship.
Birbal defines true friendship as selflessness without expectation.
Akbar travels to a distant village seeking help from the poor friend.
The poor friend offers loyalty and trust instead of material wealth.
Akbar praises the poor friend's selflessness as more valuable than gold.
The court is moved by the depth of the friendship and reflects on its value.
Birbal and Akbar reflect on their journey and what they've learned about selflessness and true friendship.
Akbar realizes that true friendship is not measured by wealth, but by the strength of one's soul.
Birbal and Ak,bar reaffirm their bond through shared wisdom and mutual respect.
Akbar acknowledges that the true merchant is not someone who sells physical goods but a person whose heart embodies selflessness and integrity.
Birbal promises to continue guiding Akbar in his quest for wisdom and understanding.
The true merchant's identity remains a mystery, but the lesson is clear: value lies in character, not possessions.
